notes.1: (tn, Heb): “The word of the Lord which came to.”
notes.2: (tn, Heb): “in the days of.” The words “Zephaniah delivered this message” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

notes.3: (tn): The Hebrew text combines the infinitive absolute of אָסַף (’asaf, “gather up, sweep away”) with a Hiphil prefixed first person form of סוּף (suf, “come to an end”; see Jer 8:13 for the same combination). This can be translated literally, “Sweeping away, I will bring to an end.” Some prefer to emend the text so that the infinitive and finite form of the verb are from the same root (“I will certainly sweep away,” if from אָסַף [cf. NEB, NIV, NRSV]; “I will certainly bring to an end,” if from סוּף). For a discussion of proposals see J. J. M. Roberts, Nahum, Habakkuk, and Zephaniah (OTL), 167, 169.

rashi.heb:
*אסוף אסף.* 
לשון כליון כמו (שופטים יח) ואספת את נפשך דמיכה ואל"ף חסרה בתיבה שנייה שהרי היה לו לכתוב אאסוף אבל יש כאלה הרבה כמו לא יהל שם ערבי (ישעיה יג) שהוא כמו לא יאהל:
rashi.eng: *I will totally destroy.* An expression of destruction, as in (Jud. 18:25) “and you will lose your life,” mentioned regarding Micah. The “aleph” is defective in the second word, for it should have been written אֶאֱסֹף There are many [defective alephs] like these, as in (Isa. 13:20) “no Arab shall pitch his tent there,” which is like יֶאֱהַל.

notes.4: (tn, Heb): “And the stumbling blocks [or, “ruins”] with the evil”; or “the things that make the evil stumble.” The line does not appear in the original form of the LXX; it may be a later scribal addition. The present translation assumes the “stumbling blocks” are idolatrous images of animals, birds, and fish. See J. J. M. Roberts, Nahum, Habakkuk, and Zephaniah (OTL), 167, and Adele Berlin, Zephaniah (AB), 73-74.

rashi.heb:
*והמכשלות את הרשעים.* 
הם העכו"ם:
rashi.eng: *and the stumbling blocks with the wicked.* They are the pagan deities.

notes.6: (tn, Heb): “I will stretch out my hand against,” is an idiom for hostile action.
notes.7: (map): For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.
notes.10: (tn, Heb): “name.” Here the “name” is figurative for the memory of those who bear it.
notes.11: (tc, Heb): “of the pagan priests and priests.” The first word (כְּמָרִים, k�marim) refers to idolatrous priests in its two other appearances in the OT (2 Kgs 23:5, Hos 10:5), while the second word (כֹּהֲנִים, kohanim) is the normal term for “priest” and is used of both legitimate and illegitimate priests in the OT. It is likely that the second term, which is omitted in the LXX, is a later scribal addition to the Hebrew text, defining the extremely rare word that precedes (see J. J. M. Roberts, Nahum, Habakkuk, and Zephaniah [OTL], 167-68; cf. also NEB, NRSV). Some argue that both words are original; among the modern English versions that include both are NASB and NIV. Possibly the first word refers to outright pagan priests, while the second has in view once-legitimate priests of the Lord who had drifted into idolatrous practices. Another option is found in Adele Berlin, who translates, “the idolatrous priests among the priests,” understanding the second word as giving the general category of which the idolatrous priests are a part (Zephaniah [AB 25A], 75).

rashi.heb:
*את שאר הבעל.* 
שלא תהא שארית לזכרונו:
rashi.eng: *the remnant of Baal.* that there shall be no remnant of its remembrance.

rashi.heb:
*הכמרים עם הכהנים.* 
פלחיהון עם כומריהם:
rashi.eng: *the name of the idolatrous priests with the ancillary priests.* Their worshippers with their priests.

notes.12: (tn): The words “I will remove” are repeated from v. 4b for stylistic reasons. In the Hebrew text vv. 4b-6 contain a long list of objects for the verb “I will remove” in v. 4b. In the present translation a new sentence was begun at the beginning of v. 5 in keeping with the tendency of contemporary English to use shorter sentences.
notes.13: (tn, Heb): “those who worship on their roofs the host of heaven.” The “host of heaven” included the sun, moon, planets, and stars, all of which were deified in the ancient Near East.
notes.14: (tc): The MT reads, “those who worship, those who swear allegiance to the Lord.” The original form of the LXX omits the phrase “those who worship”; it may have been accidentally repeated from the preceding line. J. J. M. Roberts prefers to delete as secondary the phrase “those who swear allegiance” (J. J. M. Roberts, Nahum, Habakkuk, and Zephaniah [OTL], 168).
notes.16: (tn): The referent of “their king” is unclear. It may refer sarcastically to a pagan god (perhaps Baal) worshiped by the people. Some English versions (cf. NEB, NASB, NRSV) prefer to emend the text to “Milcom,” the name of an Ammonite god (following some LXX mss, Syriac, and Vulgate) or “Molech,” a god to whom the Israelites offered their children (cf. NIV, NLT). For a discussion of the options, see Adele Berlin, Zephaniah (AB 25A), 75-77.

rashi.heb:
*ואת הנשבעים לה'.* 
וחוזרים ונשבעים במלכם בעכו"ם שלהם עושין עכו"ם עיקר לומר אם אין אתה מאמין בשבועת ה' הריני נשבע לך בעכו"ם:
rashi.eng: *who swear by the Lord.* and go back and swear by their king, their pagan deity. They make the pagan deity the main one, saying, “If you do not believe the oath by God, I swear to you by the pagan deity.”

notes.18: (tn, Heb): “who do not seek the Lord and do not inquire of him.” The present translation assumes the first verb refers to praying for divine help and the second to seeking his revealed will through an oracle. Note the usage of the two verbs in 2 Chr 20:3-4.

notes.19: (tn, Heb): “Lord Lord.” The phrase אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה (adonai y�hvih) is customarily rendered by Jewish tradition as “Lord God.”
notes.20: (tn, Heb): “the day of the Lord.” The origin of the concept of “the day of the Lord” is uncertain. It may have originated in the ancient Near Eastern idea of the sovereign’s day of conquest, where a king would boast that he had concluded an entire military campaign in a single day (see D. Stuart, “The Sovereign’s Day of Conquest,” BASOR 221 [1976]: 159-64). In the OT the expression is applied to several acts of divine judgment, some historical and others still future (see A. J. Everson, “The Days of Yahweh,” JBL 93 [1974]: 329-37). In the OT the phrase first appears in Amos (assuming that Amos predates Joel and Obadiah), where it seems to refer to a belief on the part of the northern kingdom that God would intervene on Israel’s behalf and judge the nation’s enemies. Amos affirms that the Lord’s day of judgment is indeed approaching, but he declares that it will be a day of disaster, not deliverance, for Israel. Here in Zephaniah, the “day of the Lord” includes God’s coming judgment of Judah, as well as a more universal outpouring of divine anger.
notes.22: (tn, Heb): “a sacrifice.” This same word also occurs in the following verse. Because a sacrificial meal presupposes the slaughter of animals, it is used here as a metaphor of the bloody judgment to come.

rashi.heb:
*הקדיש קרואיו.* 
זימן חיילותיו ליום מועד:
rashi.eng: *He has invited His guests.* He prepared His armies for the appointed day.

notes.25: (sn): The very dress of the royal court, foreign styles of clothing, revealed the degree to which Judah had assimilated foreign customs.

rashi.heb:
*מלבוש נכרי.* 
תכשיטי עכו"ם:
rashi.eng: *gentile garb.* Ornaments of the idols.

notes.26: (sn): The point of the statement all who hop over the threshold is unclear. A ritual or superstition associated with the Philistine god Dagon may be in view (see 1 Sam 5:5).
notes.27: (tn): The referent of “their master” is unclear. The king or a pagan god may be in view.
notes.28: (tn, Heb): “who fill…with violence and deceit.” The expression “violence and deceit” refers metonymically to the wealth taken by oppressive measures.

rashi.heb:
*הדולג על המפתן.* 
ת"י דמהלכין בנימוסי פלשתאי, שלא היו דורכים על מפתן דגון שנא' על כן לא ידרכו כהני דגון וגו' (שמואל א ה):
rashi.eng: *who leaps over the threshold.* Jonathan renders: who follows the customs of the Philistines, who would not step on the threshold of Dagon, as it is stated (I Sam. 5:5): “Therefore, the priests of Dagon… do not tread, etc.”

notes.29: (tn): The words “will go up” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
notes.30: (sn): The Fish Gate was located on Jerusalem’s north side (cf. 2 Chr 33:14; Neh 3:3; 12:39).
notes.31: (tn, Heb): “from the second area.” This may refer to an area northwest of the temple where the rich lived (see Adele Berlin, Zephaniah [AB 25A], 86; cf. NASB, NRSV “the Second Quarter”; NIV “the New Quarter”).

rashi.heb:
*משער הדגים.* 
ת"י מתרע נוניא ושער היה בירושלים וכך שמו:
rashi.eng: *from the fish gate.* Jonathan renders: from the gate of the fish; there was a gate in Jerusalem called by that name.

rashi.heb:
*מן המשנה.* 
משער העופות שהוא שני לו:
rashi.eng: *from the second gate.* from the gate of the fowl, which was second to it [the fish gate].

notes.33: (tn, Heb): “in the Mortar.” The Hebrew term מַכְתֵּשׁ (makhtesh, “mortar”) is apparently here the name of a low-lying area where economic activity took place.
notes.34: (tn): Or perhaps “Canaanites.” Cf. BDB 489 s.v. I and II כְּנַעֲנִי. Translators have rendered the term either as “the merchant people” (KJV, NKJV), “the traders” (NRSV), “merchants” (NEB, NIV), or, alternatively, “the people of Canaan” (NASB).
notes.37: (tn, Heb): “be cut off.” In the Hebrew text of v. 11b the perfect verbal forms emphasize the certainty of the judgment, speaking of it as if it were already accomplished.

rashi.heb:
*יושבי המכתש.* 
נחלא דקדרון שעמוקה כמכתשת זה ת"י. ומדרש אגדה:
rashi.eng: *you inhabitants of Maktesh.* The Kidron Valley, which is as deep as a mortar. This is according to Targum Jonathan.

rashi.heb:
*משער הדגים.* 
זו עכו הנתונה בחיקו של הים ששם נצודים דגים הרבה:
rashi.eng: *from the fish gate.* This is Acre, situated in the bosom of the sea, where many fish are caught.

rashi.heb:
*מן המשנה.* 
לוד שהיא משנה לירושלים:
rashi.eng: *from the Mishneh.* This is Lod, which is second to Jerusalem.

rashi.heb:
*מהגבעות.* 
זו צפורי שיושבת בראשי ההרים כצפור:
rashi.eng: *from the hills.* This is Sepphoris, which is situated at the tops of the mountains like a bird.

rashi.heb:
*יושבי המכתש.* 
זו טבריא שעמוקה מכל ארץ ישראל:
rashi.eng: *[11] inhabitants of Maktesh.* This is Tiberias, which is deeper than all of [the rest of] the land of Israel.

rashi.heb:
*כי נדמה כל עם כנען.* 
ת"י ארי אתר כל עמא דדמי עובדיהון לעובדי עמא דארעא דכנען:
rashi.eng: *for the entire people of Canaan is cut off.* Jonathan renders: For the entire nation, whose deeds resemble the deeds of the people of the land of Canaan, has been broken.

rashi.heb:
*כל נטילי כסף.* 
כל עתירי נכסיא טעוני משא כסף וזהב כמו (משלי כ״ז:ג׳) כובד האבן ונטל החול ל' משא:
rashi.eng: *all those laden with silver.* Jonathan renders: All those wealthy with property, laden with a burden of silver and gold; as in (Prov. 27:3) “The weight of stone, the burden of sand” an expression of a burden.

notes.38: (tn, Heb): “who thicken on their sediment.” The imagery comes from wine making, where the wine, if allowed to remain on the sediment too long, will thicken into syrup. The image suggests that the people described here were complacent in their sinful behavior and interpreted the delay in judgment as divine apathy.
notes.40: (tn, Heb): “The Lord does not do good nor does he do evil.”

rashi.heb:
*אחפש את ירושלים בנרות.* 
אדקדק בעונותיהם:
rashi.eng: *I will search Jerusalem with candles.* I will judge their iniquities strictly.

rashi.heb:
*הקופאים.* 
הצפים על שמריהם ויצף הברזל (מלכים ב ו׳:ו׳) מתרגמינן וקפא פרזלא:
rashi.eng: *who are settled.* float on their lees. [As in] (II Kings 6:6) “And the axe blade floated,” rendered in Aramaic: וּקְפָא פַרְזְלָה.

rashi.heb:
*האומרים בלבבם לא ייטיב ה'.* 
לעושי רצונו:
rashi.eng: *who say in their heart, “The Lord shall do neither good…”.* to those who obey His will.

rashi.heb:
*ולא ירע.* 
לעוברי רצונו:
rashi.eng: *nor harm.* to those who transgress His will.

notes.41: (tn, Heb): “The great day of the Lord.” The words “of judgment” are supplied in the translation here and later in this verse for clarity. See the note on the expression “day of judgment” in v. 7.
notes.42: (tn, Heb): “the sound of the day of the Lord, bitter [is] one crying out there, a warrior.” The present translation does four things: (1) It takes מַר (mar, “bitter”) with what precedes (contrary to the accentuation of the MT). (2) It understands the participle צָרַח (tsarakh, “cry out in battle”) as verbal with “warrior” as its subject. (3) It takes שָׁם (sham, “there”) in a temporal sense, meaning “then, at that time.” (4) It understands “warrior” as collective.

rashi.heb:
*מר צורח שם גבור.* 
הגבור יצרח שם בקול מר:
rashi.eng: *wherein the mighty man cries bitterly.* The mighty man will cry out with a bitter voice.

notes.43: (tn, Heb): “a day of wrath.” The word “God’s” is supplied in the translation for clarification.

rashi.heb:
*יום שואה.* 
לשון שממון:
rashi.eng: *a day of ruin.* , an expression of desolation.

rashi.heb:
*ומשואה.* 
שממון יותר:
rashi.eng: *and desolation.* A greater degree of desolation.

notes.44: (tn, Heb): “a ram’s horn.” By metonymy the Hebrew text mentions the trumpet (“ram’s horn”) in place of the sound it produces (“trumpet blasts”).
notes.45: (sn): This description of the day of the Lord consists of an initial reference to anger, followed by four pairs of synonyms. The joining of synonyms in this way emphasizes the degree of the characteristic being described. The first two pairs focus on the distress and ruin that judgment will bring; the second two pairs picture this day of judgment as being very dark (darkness) and exceedingly overcast (gloom). The description concludes with the pairing of two familiar battle sounds, the blast on the ram’s horn (trumpet blasts) and the war cries of the warriors (battle cries).
notes.46: (tn, Heb): “against.” The words “judgment will fall” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

notes.47: (tn): “The people” refers to mankind in general (see vv. 2-3) or more specifically to the residents of Judah (see vv. 4-13).
notes.49: (tn): Some take the referent of “flesh” to be more specific here; cf. NEB (“bowels”), NAB (“brains”), NIV (“entrails”).
notes.50: (tn): The words “will be scattered” are supplied in the translation for clarity based on the parallelism with “will be poured out” in the previous line.

rashi.heb:
*והצרותי לאדם.* 
לישראל הקרויים אדם:
rashi.eng: *And I will bring distress upon men.* Upon Israel, who is called “man.”

rashi.heb:
*ולחומם.* 
בשרם ול' ערבי בשר קורין אל לחם:
rashi.eng: *and their flesh.* their flesh. In Arabic, flesh is called al laham.

rashi.heb:
*כגללים.* 
רעי:
rashi.eng: *like dung.* dung.

notes.51: (tn): Or “land” (cf. NEB). This same word also occurs at the end of the present verse.
notes.54: (tn, Heb): “complete destruction, even terror, he will make.”
notes.55: (tn): It is not certain where the Lord’s words end and the prophet’s words begin. It is possible that Zephaniah begins speaking in the middle of v. 17 or at the beginning of v. 18 (note the third person pronouns referring to the Lord).

notes.56: (tn): The Hebrew text combines a Hitpolel imperative of קָשַׁשׁ (qashash) with a Qal imperative of the same root. Elsewhere this root appears in the polel stem with the meaning “gather stubble.” Zephaniah’s command is ironic, implying the people are like stubble or straw. As such, they are vulnerable to the Lord’s fiery judgment that will quickly consume them (see 1:18). See Adele Berlin, Zephaniah (AB 25A), 96.
notes.57: (tn): Some relate this word to an Aramaic cognate meaning “to be ashamed.” With the negative particle it would then mean “unashamed” (cf. NIV “shameful”; NRSV “shameless”). However, elsewhere in biblical Hebrew the verb means “to desire,” or with the negative particle “undesirable.” Cf. also NEB “unruly.”

rashi.heb:
*התקוששו.* 
התלקטו ואספו יחד כמו לקושש קש (שמות ה):
rashi.eng: *Gather yourselves together.* Gather and assemble together as in (Exod. 5:12) “To Gather a gathering.”

rashi.heb:
*וקושו.* 
מעשיכם השוו מעשיכם לדעת קונכם, ורז"ל דרשו קשוט עצמך ואח"כ קשוט אחרים עשו שניהם לשון היקש אדם המשוה עצמו ומישר דרכו:
rashi.eng: *gather together.* your deeds. Conform your deeds to the will of Your Maker.

rashi.heb:
*הגוי לא נכסף.* 
ת"י דלא חמד למיתב לאורייתא:
rashi.eng: *O nation that has no desire.* That has no desire to return to the Torah.

notes.58: (tn, Heb): “before the giving birth of a decree.” For various alternative readings, see J. J. M. Roberts, Nahum, Habakkuk, and Zephaniah (OTL), 187-88.
notes.59: (tn): The second half of the line reads literally, “like chaff it passes by a day.” The translation above assumes the “day” is the brief time God is giving the nation to repent. The comparison of this quickly passing opportunity to chaff is consistent with the straw imagery of v. 1.
notes.60: (tn, Heb): “the fury of the anger of the Lord.” The synonyms are combined to emphasize the extreme degree of the Lord’s anger.
notes.61: (tn, Heb): “comes upon.” This phrase occurs twice in this verse.

rashi.heb:
*בטרם לדת חוק.* 
לפני בא הגזירה:
rashi.eng: *before the decree is born.* Before the arrival of the decree.

rashi.heb:
*כמוץ עבר.* 
הרי זה מקרא קצר כמוץ העובר מלפני רוח וכעשן העובר מלפני השמש וזהו תרגומו של עבר יום כך ת"י תהוון דמן לכמוצא דנשב ביה רוחא וכתננא דעדי מן קדם יומא, נ"א כטולא דעדו וכו' זהו ל' צל:
rashi.eng: *as chaff that passes…the sun.* This is an ellipsis for, “As chaff that passes from before the wind, and as smoke that passes from before the sun.” This is the translation of עָבַר יוֹם, that passes the sun. In this manner, Jonathan renders: And you shall be like the chaff that the wind blows, like smoke that passes from before the sun. Another version: and like the shadow that passes, etc.; this is an expression of a shadow.

notes.62: (tn, Heb): “seek the Lord,” but “favor” seems to be implied from the final line of the verse.
notes.63: (tn): Or “poor.” The precise referent of this Hebrew term is unclear. The word may refer to the economically poor or to the spiritually humble.
notes.64: (tn): The present translation assumes the Hebrew term מִשְׁפָּט (mishpat) here refers to God’s covenantal requirements and is a synonym for the Law. The word can mean “justice” and could refer more specifically to the principles of justice contained in the Law. In this case the phrase could be translated, “who have promoted the justice God demands.”
notes.67: (tn, Heb): “hidden.” Cf. NEB “it may be that you will find shelter”; NRSV “perhaps you may be hidden.”

notes.69: (tn): There is a sound play here in the Hebrew text: the name Gaza (עַזָּה, ’azzah) sounds like the word translated “deserted” (עֲזוּבָה, ’azuvah).
notes.71: (tn, Heb): “[As for] Ashdod, at noon they will drive her away.” The reference to noon may suggest a sudden, quick defeat (see Jer 6:4; 15:8).
notes.72: (tn, Heb): “uprooted.” There is a sound play here in the Hebrew text: the name “Ekron” (עֶקְרוֹן, ’eqron) sounds like the word translated “uprooted” (תֵּעָקֵר, te’aqer).

rashi.heb:
*כי עזה עזובה תהיה.* 
כי אם תעשו כן אפקוד על שכיניכם הרעים פלשת ועמון ומואב כמו שהנביא מסדרן והולך:
rashi.eng: *For Gaza shall be deserted.* For, if you will do so, [as in verse 1,] I will visit retribution upon your evil neighbors; Philistia, Ammon, and Moab. The prophet proceeds to mention them [the neighbors] in [geographical] order.

rashi.heb:
*בצהרים יגרשוה.* 
אשדוד שמה ובצהרים אשר ישוד בה קטב יגרשוה ותהי שדודה, ד"א בצהרים יגרשוה מקום מרעה צאן היה וצהרים קשה לצאת בו צאן וכן הוא אומר איכה תרביץ בצהרים (שיר השירים א׳:ז׳):
rashi.eng: *Ashdod at noon they shall drive her out.* Her name is Ashdod, and, at noon, when the destruction wastes, they shall drive her out, and she shall be plundered. Another explanation. At noon they shall drive her out. [Ashdod] was a place to pasture sheep, and it is hard for the sheep to go out at noontime; so Scripture says (Song 1:7): “How do you make them lie down at noon?”

notes.73: (tn, Heb): “Kerethites,” a people settled alongside the Philistines in the coastal areas of southern Palestine (cf. 1 Sam 30:14; Ezek 25:16). They originally came from the island of Crete.
notes.74: (tn, Heb): “Woe, inhabitants of the coast of the sea, nation of Kerethites.” The Hebrew term הוֹי (hoy, “ah, woe”), is used to mourn the dead and express outwardly one’s sorrow (see 1 Kgs 13:30; Jer 22:18; 34:5). By using it here the prophet mourns in advance the downfall of the Philistines, thereby emphasizing the certainty of their demise (“as good as dead”). Some argue the word does not have its earlier connotation here and is simply an attention-getting interjection, equivalent to “Hey!”
notes.75: (tn, Heb): “the word of the Lord is against you.”
notes.76: (tn, Heb): “I will destroy you so there is no inhabitant [remaining].”

rashi.heb:
*חבל הים.* 
ספר ימא ול' חבל מדת הקרקע היא שמודדין בחבל כלומר הסמוכים לים:
rashi.eng: *the seacoast.* the border of the sea. The expression חֶבֶל is a measure of land that they measured with a rope, i.e., those close to the sea.

rashi.heb:
*גוי כרתים.* 
ת"י עמא דמחייבין לאישתצאה ומי הן יושבי חבל הים כנען ארץ פלשתים כי פלשתים יושבים על שפת הים האחרון במערב' של א"י בתוך מצרי תחומיה ואף שדורשו יונתן לכליה גוי כרתים מדינה היא בפלשתים ושמה כרתי וכן הוא אומר בצקלג אנחנו פשטנו על נגב הכרתי ועל אשר ליהודה ות"י על דרום כרתי ולמטה כתוב בכל השלל הגדול אשר לקחו מארץ פלשתים ומארץ יהודה:
rashi.eng: *the nation of Cherethites.* the people liable to destruction. Who are the inhabitants of the seacoast of Canaan, the land of the Philistines? The Philistines, who dwell on the coast of the western sea, in the west of Eretz lsrael, within its boundaries. Although Jonathan explains this phrase homiletically as [the nation of] destruction, the nation of the Cherethites is a province of the Philistines; its name is Cherethi. So Scripture states (I Sam. 30:14) regarding Ziklag: “We made a raid upon the south of the Cherethites, etc.” Jonathan translates: on the south of Cherethi. Below (ibid. 30:16) it is written: “Because of all the great spoil which they had taken from the land of the Philistines and from the land of Judah.”

notes.77: (tn): The NIV here supplies the phrase “where the Kerethites dwell” (“Kerethites” is translated in v. 5 as “the people who came from Crete”) as an interpretive gloss, but this phrase is not in the MT. The NAB likewise reads “the coastland of the Cretans,” supplying “Cretans” here.
notes.78: (tn): The Hebrew phrase here is נְוֹת כְּרֹת (n�vot k�rot). The first word is probably a plural form of נָוָה (navah, “pasture”). The meaning of the second word is unclear. It may be a synonym of the preceding word (cf. NRSV “pastures, meadows for shepherds”); there is a word כַּר (kar, “pasture”) in biblical Hebrew, but elsewhere it forms its plural with a masculine ending. Some have suggested the meaning “wells” or “caves” used as shelters (cf. NEB “shepherds’ huts”); in this case, one might translate, “The seacoast will be used for pasturelands; for shepherds’ wells/caves.”

rashi.heb:
*נות כרות רועים.* 
נוה עראי שיכרו בה הרועים לחם בבוקר כרות לשון ויכרה להם כירה גדולה (מלכים ב ו׳:כ״ג):
rashi.eng: *breakfast nooks for shepherds.* a temporary dwelling where the shepherds eat bread in the morning. כְּרֹת is an expression related to (II Kings 6:23) “He prepared for them a lavish feast.”

notes.79: (tn, Heb): “the remnant of the house of Judah.”
notes.80: (tn): Or “the coast will belong to the remnant of the house of Judah.”
notes.81: (tc, Heb): “on them,” but the antecedent of the masculine pronoun is unclear. It may refer back to the “pasture lands,” though that noun is feminine. It is preferable to emend the text from עֲלֵיהֶם (’alehem) to עַל־הַיָּם (’al-hayyam, “by the sea”) an emendation that assumes a misdivision and transposition of letters in the MT (cf. NEB “They shall pasture their flocks by the sea”). See J. J. M. Roberts, Nahum, Habakkuk, and Zephaniah (OTL), 192.
notes.82: (tn): The referent of the pronominal subject (“they”) is unclear. It may refer (1) to the shepherds (in which case the first verb should be translated, “pasture their sheep,” cf. NEB), or (2) to the Judahites occupying the area, who are being compared to sheep (cf. NIV, “there they will find pasture”).
notes.84: (tn): Traditionally, “restore their captivity,” i.e., bring back their captives, but it is more likely the expression means “restore their fortunes” in a more general sense (cf. NEB, NASB, NIV, NRSV).

rashi.heb:
*והיה חבל לשארית בית יהודה.* 
והיה אותו הגבול גורל לשארית בני יהודה חבל זה ל' גורל הוא וכן ת"י ויהי עדבא לשארא דבית יהודה:
rashi.eng: *And it shall be a lot for the remnant of the house of Judah.* And that border shall be a lot for the remnant. This חֶבֶל is an expression of a lot. In this manner, Jonathan rendered: And it shall be a lot for the remnant of the house of Judah.

notes.85: (tn, Heb): “who.” A new sentence was begun here in the translation for stylistic reasons.
notes.86: (tn, Heb): “and they made great [their mouth?] against their territory.” Other possible translation options include (1) “they enlarged their own territory” (cf. NEB) and (2) “they bragged about [the size] of their own territory.”

rashi.heb:
*אשר חרפו את עמי.* 
כשהיו מוליכין ישראל בגולה לצד ארץ כשדים והיו עוברין דרך עמון ומואב ורואים ישראל בוכים וגונחים וצועקין היו מונין אותן ואומרים מה לכם להיות סגופים מה תבכו הלא לבית אביכם אתם הולכים בעבר הנהר ישבו אבותיכם מעולם:
rashi.eng: *who taunted My people.* When [the people of] Israel were being led into exile toward the land of the Chaldeans, and they were passing through Ammon and Moab, and they would see Israel weeping, sighing, and crying out, they would taunt them and say, “Why are you suffering? Aren’t you going to your father’s house? Your fathers dwelt on the other side of the river from earliest times.” (Josh. 24:2)

rashi.heb:
*ויגדילו על גבולם.* 
ויתגאו על גבולם:
rashi.eng: *and they aggrandized themselves on their border.* And they acted haughtily on their border.

notes.87: (tn): The Hebrew text reads מִמְשַׁק חָרוּל (mimshaq kharul, “[?] of weeds”). The meaning of the first word is unknown. The present translation (“They will be overrun by weeds”) is speculative, based on the general sense of the context. For a defense of “overrun” on linguistic grounds, see R. D. Patterson, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah (WEC), 347. Cf. NEB “a pile of weeds”; NIV “a place of weeds”; NRSV “a land possessed by nettles.”
notes.88: (tn): The Hebrew text reads וּמִכְרֵה־מֶלַח (umikhreh-melakh, “and a [?] of salt”). The meaning of the first word is unclear, though “pit” (NASB, NIV, NRSV; NKJV “saltpit”), “mine,” and “heap” (cf. NEB “a rotting heap of saltwort”) are all options. The words “filled with” are supplied for clarification.
notes.90: (tn, Heb): “them.” The actual object of the plundering, “their belongings,” has been specified in the translation for clarity.
notes.91: (tn, Heb): “[the] nation.” For clarity the “nation” has been specified as “Judah” in the translation.

rashi.heb:
*כי מואב כסדום תהיה.* 
גם אתם לקדמתכ' תשובו לוט אביכם לא מסדום היה:
rashi.eng: *for Moab shall be like Sodom.* You, too, shall return to your previous dwelling. Was not your father, Lot, from Sodom?

rashi.heb:
*ממשק חרול.* 
השמעת קול כמו משק גבים (ישעיה לג) ואף מ"ם הראשונה יסוד היא בתיבה כמו ממשח הסוכך (יחזקאל כ״ח:י״ד) ממשק חרול השמעת קול חרולים הגדילים שם מאין עובר והן נוקשין זו על זו ומשמיעות קול:
rashi.eng: *a rattling of nettles.* The sound made by the nettles growing there because there are no passersby, and they knock against each other and make sounds.

rashi.heb:
*ומכרה מלח.* 
מקום כריית מלח:
rashi.eng: *and a salt mine.* a place for digging salt.

notes.92: (tn, Heb): “this is for them in place of their arrogance.”
notes.93: (tn, Heb): “made great [their mouth?] against” (cf. the last phrase of v. 8).

notes.96: (tn): The meaning of this rare Hebrew word is unclear. If the meaning is indeed “weaken,” then this line may be referring to the reduction of these gods’ territory through conquest (see Adele Berlin, Zephaniah [AB 25A], 110-11). Cf. NEB “reduce to beggary”; NASB “starve”; NIV “when he destroys”; NRSV “shrivel.”
notes.97: (tn, Heb): “and all the coastlands of the nations will worship [or, “bow down”] to him, each from his own place.”

rashi.heb:
*כי רזה.* 
התיש כחם:
rashi.eng: *for He weakened.* He weakened their strength.

rashi.heb:
*וישתחוו לו.* 
כשיראו שנתקלקלו יראתן:
rashi.eng: *and… shall prostrate himself to Him.* when they see that their deity has deteriorated.

notes.98: (sn): Though there is no formal introduction, these words are apparently spoken by the Lord (note my sword).
notes.99: (tn, Heb): “Cushites.” This is traditionally assumed to refer to people from the region south of Egypt, i.e., Nubia or northern Sudan, referred to as “Ethiopia” by classical authors (not the more recent Abyssinia).
notes.100: (tn, Heb): “Also you Cushites, who lie dead by my sword.”

rashi.heb:
*גם אתם כושים.* 
כשגלו שם ישראל מעבר לנהרי כוש:
rashi.eng: *You, too, Cushites.* When Israel was exiled there to the other side of the rivets of Cush.

notes.101: (tn, Heb): “He”; the referent (the Lord) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
notes.102: (tn, Heb): “he will stretch out his hand against the north.”

rashi.heb:
*על צפון.* 
אשור בצפון אצל בבל:
rashi.eng: *on the north.* Assyria is on the north, neighboring on Babylon.

rashi.heb:
*נינוה.* 
הוא ראש לאשור:
rashi.eng: *Nineveh.* That is the capital of Assyria.

notes.104: (tn, Heb): “flocks.” The Hebrew word can refer to both flocks of sheep and herds of cattle.
notes.105: (tn, Heb): “[and] all the wild animals of a nation.” How גוֹי (goy, “nation”) relates to what precedes is unclear. It may be a corruption of another word. See J. J. M. Roberts, Nahum, Habakkuk, and Zephaniah (OTL), 193.
notes.106: (tn): The Hebrew text reads here גַּם־קָאַת גַּם־קִפֹּד (gam-qa’at gam-qippod). The term קָאַת refers to some type of bird (see Lev 11:18; Deut 14:17) that was typically found near ruins (Isa 34:11); one of the most common translations is “owl” (cf. NEB “horned owl”; NIV, NRSV “desert owl”; contra NASB “pelican”). The term קִפֹּד may also refer to a type of bird (cf. NEB “ruffed bustard”; NIV, NRSV “screech owl”). Some suggest a rodent may be in view (cf. NASB “hedgehog”); this is not unreasonable, for a rodent or some other small animal would be able to sleep in the tops of pillars which would be lying in the ruins of the fallen buildings.
notes.107: (tn, Heb): “a sound will sing in the window.” If some type of owl is in view, “hoot” is a more appropriate translation (cf. NEB, NRSV).
notes.108: (tn, Heb): “rubble [will be] on the threshold.” “Rubble” translates the Hebrew word חֹרֶב (khorev, “desolation”). Some emend to עֹרֵב (’orev, “raven”) following the LXX and Vulgate; Adele Berlin translates, “A voice shall shriek from the window – a raven at the sill” (Zephaniah [AB 25A], 104).
notes.109: (tn): The meaning of the Hebrew word translated “cedar work” (so NASB, NRSV) is unclear; NIV has “the beams of cedar.”
notes.110: (tn, Heb): “one will expose.” The subject is probably indefinite, though one could translate, “for he [i.e., God] will lay bare.”

rashi.heb:
*כל חיתו גוי.* 
כל בהמות הגוים:
rashi.eng: *all the beasts of the nations.* all the cattle of the nations.

rashi.heb:
*קאת וקפוד.* 
עופות:
rashi.eng: *the pelican and the owl.* birds.

rashi.heb: *וקפוד.*
rashi.eng: *owl.* a bird that flies at night (chouette in French), an owl.

rashi.heb:
*בכפתוריה.* 
פומל"ש שבראש הגג:
rashi.eng: *in its lintels.* rounded knobs on the top of the roof; pomels in French.

rashi.heb:
*חורב בסף.* 
החורבן יהיה ניכר בספי הבית:
rashi.eng: *Their voice shall sing in the window.* The voice of the birds chirping in the windows.

rashi.heb:
*קול ישורר בחלון.* 
קול העופות מצפצפים בחלונות:
rashi.eng: *desolation, in the doorpost.* The desolation shall be discernible in the doorposts of the house.

rashi.heb:
*כי ארזה ערה.* 
כי ארזיה עקר ושרש כמו ערו ערו (תהלים קלו) וי"ת וטללה סתרו הוא גג הבית הספון בארז שאפי' בתי אבנים מסככין בנסרים של עץ:
rashi.eng: *for the cedarwork has been destroyed.* For he has uprooted its cedars, as in (Ps. 137:7) “Raze it, raze it.” Jonathan rendered: And they demolished its roof. That is the roof of the house that is ceiled with cedar; even stone houses are ceiled with boards of wood.

notes.113: (tn, Heb): “the one who says in her heart.”
notes.114: (tn, Heb): “I [am], and besides me there is no other.”
notes.116: (sn): Hissing (or whistling) and shaking the fist were apparently ways of taunting a defeated foe or an object of derision in the culture of the time.

rashi.heb:
*ואפסי.* 
ואפס זולתי:
rashi.eng: *and there is none besides me.* וְאַפְסִי

notes.117: (tn): The present translation assumes מֹרְאָה (mor’ah) is derived from רֹאִי (ro’i,“excrement”; see Jastrow 1436 s.v. רֳאִי). The following participle, “stained,” supports this interpretation (cf. NEB “filthy and foul”; NRSV “soiled, defiled”). Another option is to derive the form from מָרָה (marah, “to rebel”); in this case the term should be translated “rebellious” (cf. NASB, NIV “rebellious and defiled”). This idea is supported by v. 2. For discussion of the two options, see HALOT 630 s.v. I מרא and J. J. M. Roberts, Nahum, Habakkuk, and Zephaniah (OTL), 206.
notes.118: (tn, Heb): “Woe, soiled and stained one, oppressive city.” The verb “is finished” is supplied in the second line. On the Hebrew word הוֹי (hoy, “ah, woe”), see the note on the word “dead” in 2:5. The following verses show that Jerusalem, personified as a woman (“she”), is the referent.

rashi.heb:
*הוי מוראה ונגאלה.* 
עד עכשיו דבר בנינוה ועכשיו חוזר על ירושלים הוי שתהא לבז ולסחי כרואי ותהא מגואלת בצחן עוונה:
rashi.eng: *Woe to her who is filthy and polluted.* Until now, Zephaniah was speaking of Ninveh, but now he refers to Jerusalem: Woe to her who is destined to be plundered and sullied like dung. It will be polluted with the filth of its iniquity.

rashi.heb:
*מוראה.* 
כמו מוראתו (ויקרא א) ושמתיך כרואי (נחום ג):
rashi.eng: *filthy.* as in (Lev. 1:16) “its crop” ; and (Nahum 3:6) “And I will make you like dung.”

rashi.heb:
*העיר היונה.* 
כיונה פותה אין לב:
rashi.eng: *the dove like city.* Like a silly dove, without a heart.

notes.119: (tn, Heb): “she does not hear a voice” Refusing to listen is equated with disobedience.
notes.120: (tn, Heb): “she does not receive correction.” The Hebrew phrase, when negated, refers elsewhere to rejecting verbal advice (Jer 17:23; 32:33; 35:13) and refusing to learn from experience (Jer 2:30; 5:3).
notes.121: (tn, Heb): “draw near to.” The present translation assumes that the expression “draw near to” refers to seeking God’s will (see 1 Sam 14:36).

notes.123: (tn, Heb): “her princes in her midst are roaring lions.” The metaphor has been translated as a simile (“as fierce as”) for clarity.
notes.125: (tn, Heb): “her judges [are] wolves of the evening,” that is, wolves that prowl at night. The translation assumes an emendation to עֲרָבָה (’aravah, “desert”). For a discussion of this and other options, see Adele Berlin, Zephaniah (AB 25A), 128. The metaphor has been translated as a simile (“as hungry as”) for clarity.
notes.126: (tn, Heb): “they do not gnaw [a bone] at morning.” The precise meaning of the line is unclear. The statement may mean these wolves devour their prey so completely that not even a bone is left to gnaw by the time morning arrives. For a discussion of this and other options, see Adele Berlin, Zephaniah (AB 25A), 129.

rashi.heb:
*זאבי ערב.* 
הממהרים לאכול טרפם בלילה:
rashi.eng: *wolves of the evening.* who hasten to devour their prey at night.

rashi.heb:
*לא גרמו לבוקר.* 
לא השאירו אף העצמות לגרם לבוקר:
rashi.eng: *They did not leave over the bones for morning.* They did not leave over even the bones to gnaw in the morning.

notes.127: (sn): Applied to prophets, the word פֹּחֲזִים (pokhazim, “proud”) probably refers to their audacity in passing off their own words as genuine prophecies from the Lord (see Jer 23:32).
notes.128: (tn): Or “defile the temple.” These priests defile what is holy by not observing the proper distinctions between what is ritually clean and unclean (see Ezek 22:26).

rashi.heb:
*חמסו תורה.* 
לא הורו אותה לשואליהם:
rashi.eng: *they removed the Torah.* They did not teach it to those who inquired of them.

notes.130: (tn): The word “resides” is supplied for clarification.
notes.133: (tn, Heb): “at the light he is not missing.” Note that NASB (which capitalizes pronouns referring to Deity) has divided the lines differently: “Every morning He brings His justice to light; // He does not fail.”

rashi.heb:
*ה' צדיק.* 
השרה שכינתו בקרבם ולפיכך אינו יכול לראות במעשיהם הרעים כי צדיק הוא ואין עולה לפניו:
rashi.eng: *The Lord is just.* He caused His Shechinah to rest in their midst; therefore, He cannot look upon their evil deeds. He is just, and there is no injustice before Him.

rashi.heb:
*משפטו יתן לאור.* 
נותן לאור דן דין אמת לאמתו:
rashi.eng: *He brings His judgment to light.* He judges a true judgment to its absolute truth.

rashi.heb:
*ולא יודע עול בשת.* 
וכל זה לא נתנו שופטי עול שבתוכה אל לבם להתבייש מן הצדיק השוכן ביניהם:
rashi.eng: *But the one who commits injustice knows no shame.* But the unjust judges do not take it to heart, to be ashamed because of the Righteous One Who dwells among them.

notes.136: (tn): This Hebrew verb (צָדָה, tsadah) occurs only here in the OT, but its meaning is established from the context and from an Aramaic cognate.
notes.137: (tn, Heb): “so that there is no man, without inhabitant.”

rashi.heb:
*הכרתי גוים.* 
הבאתי פורענו' על העכו"ם כדי שתראו ותיראו כמו שהוא מסיים והולך אמרתי אך תראי אותי:
rashi.eng: *I have cut off nations.* I brought retribution upon the nations so that you should see and fear as He concludes, “I said, ‘Surely you will fear Me.’”

notes.139: (tn): Or “fear.” The second person verb form (“you will respect”) is feminine singular, indicating that personified Jerusalem is addressed. God’s judgment of the nations (v. 6) was an object lesson for Israel’s benefit.
notes.142: (tn, Heb): “all which I have punished her.” The precise meaning of this statement and its relationship to what precedes are unclear.
notes.143: (tn, Heb): “But they got up early, they made corrupt all their actions.” The phrase “they got up early” probably refers to their eagerness to engage in sinful activities.

rashi.heb:
*ולא יכרת מעונה.* 
ולא יחרבון מדוריה:
rashi.eng: *I said, “Surely you will fear Me… and her dwelling shall not be cut off”.* Her dwellings shall not be destroyed.

rashi.heb:
*כל אשר פקדתי עליה.* 
ולא יכרת ממנו כל הטוב אשר צויתי להביא עליה:
rashi.eng: *all that I ordained upon her.* And all the good that I ordained to bring upon her shall not be cut off from her.

notes.144: (tn): The second person verb form (“you must wait patiently”) is masculine plural, indicating that a group is being addressed. Perhaps the humble individuals addressed earlier (see 2:3) are in view. Because of Jerusalem’s sin, they must patiently wait for judgment to pass before their vindication arrives.
notes.145: (tn, Heb): “when I arise for plunder.” The present translation takes עַד (’ad) as “plunder.” Some, following the LXX, repoint the term עֵד (’ed) and translate, “as a witness” (cf. NASB, NIV, NRSV). In this case the Lord uses a legal metaphor to picture himself as testifying against his enemies. Adele Berlin takes לְעַד (l�’ad) in a temporal sense (“forever”) and translates “once and for all” (Zephaniah [AB 25A], 133).

rashi.heb:
*קומי לעד.* 
שאקום להתוועד עליכם:
rashi.eng: *That I will rise up to meet.* When I will rise to meet with you.

notes.148: (tn, Heb): “Certainly [or perhaps, “For”] then I will restore to the nations a pure lip.” I will then enable the nations to give me acceptable praise. This apparently refers to a time when the nations will reject their false idol-gods and offer genuine praise to the one true God.
notes.149: (tn, Heb): “so that all of them will call on the name of the Lord.”
notes.150: (tn, Heb): “so that [they] will serve him [with] one shoulder.”

notes.151: (tn, Heb): Or “Nubia”; “Cush.” “Cush” is traditionally assumed to refer to the region south of Egypt, i.e. Nubia or northern Sudan, referred to as “Ethiopia” by classical authors (not the more recent Abyssinia).
notes.152: (tn, Heb): “those who pray to me, the daughter of my dispersed ones.” The meaning of the phrase is unclear. Perhaps the text is corrupt at this point or a proper name should be understood. For a discussion of various options see Adele Berlin, Zephaniah (AB 25A), 134-35. It is not certain if those who pray to me refers to the converted nations or to God’s exiled covenant people.

rashi.heb:
*מעבר לנהרי כוש.* 
יובילון לי מנחה:
rashi.eng: *From the other side of the rivers of Cush.* They will bring Me an offering.

rashi.heb:
*עתרי.* 
את המתפללין אלי:
rashi.eng: *My supplicants.* those who pray to me.

rashi.heb:
*בת פוצי.* 
כנסיות נפוצותי אשר הפיצותי:
rashi.eng: *the community of My scattered ones.* The gatherings of My scattered ones, whom I scattered.

notes.153: (sn): The second person verbs and pronouns are feminine singular, indicating that personified Jerusalem is addressed here.
notes.154: (tn, Heb): “In that day you not be ashamed because of all your actions, [in] which you rebelled against me.”
notes.155: (tn, Heb): “the arrogant ones of your pride.”

rashi.heb:
*לא תבושי מכל עלילותיך.* 
כי כבר לקית ונרצה עוונך:
rashi.eng: *you shall not be ashamed of all your deeds.* Because you have already suffered, and your iniquity has been expiated.

notes.156: (tn, Heb): “needy and poor people.” The terms often refer to a socioeconomic group, but here they may refer to those who are humble in a spiritual sense.
notes.157: (tn, Heb): “and they will take refuge in the name of the Lord.” Safety in the Lord’s presence. From the time the Lord introduced his special covenant name (Yahweh) to Moses, it served as a reminder of his protective presence as Israel’s faithful deliverer.

rashi.heb:
*עם עני ודל.* 
עם ענוותן ומקבל עולבן:
rashi.eng: *a humble and poor people.* A humble people that submits to humiliation.

notes.159: (tn): The words “peacefully like sheep” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

notes.160: (sn): This phrase is used as an epithet for the city and the nation. “Daughter” may seem extraneous in English but consciously joins the various epithets and metaphors of Israel and Jerusalem as a woman, a device used to evoke sympathy from the reader.

notes.161: (tn, Heb): “your judgments,” that is, “the judgments directed against you.” The translation reflects the implications of the parallelism.

rashi.heb:
*משפטיך.* 
יסוריך יושטיצ"א בלע"ז:
rashi.eng: *your afflictions.* justice in French.

notes.162: (tn, Heb): “it will be said.” The passive construction has been translated as active for stylistic reasons.
notes.163: (tn, Heb): “your hands must not go limp.”

notes.164: (tn, Heb): “he rejoices over you with joy.”
notes.165: (tc): The MT reads, “he is silent in his love,” but this makes no sense in light of the immediately preceding and following lines. Some take the Hiphil verb form as causative (see Job 11:3) rather than intransitive and translate, “he causes [you] to be silent by his love,” that is, “he soothes [you] by his love.” The present translation follows the LXX and assumes an original reading יְחַדֵּשׁ (y�khaddesh, “he renews”) with ellipsis of the object (“you”).
notes.166: (tn, Heb): “he rejoices over you with a shout of joy.”

rashi.heb:
*גבור יושיע.* 
גבור הוא אשר יושיע מן העכו"ם:
rashi.eng: *A Mighty One will save.* He is a Mighty One, Who will save [Israel] from the enemy.

rashi.heb:
*יחריש באהבתו.* 
יכסה על פשעיך באהבתו וכן ת"י יכבוש על חובך ברחמתיה:
rashi.eng: *He will be silent in His love.* He will conceal your transgressions with His love. So did Jonathan render: He will cover your sins with His love.

notes.167: (tn, Heb): “The ones grieving from an assembly I gathered from you they were, tribute upon her, a reproach.” Any translation of this difficult verse must be provisional at best. The present translation assumes three things: (1) The preposition מִן (min) prefixed to “assembly” is causal (the individuals are sorrowing because of the assemblies or festivals they are no longer able to hold). (2) מַשְׂאֵת (mas’et) means “tribute” and refers to the exiled people being treated as the spoils of warfare (see R. D. Patterson, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah [WEC], 385-86). (3) The third feminine singular suffix refers to personified Jerusalem, which is addressed earlier in the verse (the pronominal suffix in “from you” is second feminine singular). For other interpretive options see Adele Berlin, Zephaniah (AB 25A), 146.

rashi.heb:
*נוגי ממועד.* 
אספתי את המוצאים ממועדי שלא היו משמרים שבתות וימים טובים:
rashi.eng: *Those who are removed from the appointed season.* I destroyed those removed from My appointed seasons, those who did not keep the Sabbaths and the festivals.

rashi.heb:
*אספתי.* 
כליתי:
rashi.eng: *I have destroyed.* lit., I gathered in.

rashi.heb:
*ממך היו.* 
מעמך היו:
rashi.eng: *they were of you.* They were of your people.

rashi.heb:
*משאת עליה חרפה.* 
על אותה אשמה היה לך משאת חרפה:
rashi.eng: *it was a burden of shame upon her.* That guilt was a burden of shame to you.

rashi.heb:
*נוגי.* 
לשון הוצאה כמו הגו סיגים (משלי כה) כאשר הוגה מן המסילה (שמואל ב כ׳:י״ג) ואין שורש בתיב' אלא הגימ"ל לבדה:
rashi.eng: *Those who are removed.* an expression of taking out, as in (Prov. 25:4) “Take away the dross from the silver”; and (II Sam. 20:13) “When he was removed from the highway.” The only radical letter is the “gimel.”

notes.168: (tn): The word “sheep” is supplied for clarification. As in Mic 4:6-7, the exiles are here pictured as injured and scattered sheep whom the divine shepherd rescues from danger.
notes.169: (tn, Heb): “I will make them into praise and a name, in all the earth, their shame.” The present translation assumes that “their shame” specifies “them” and that “name” stands here for a good reputation.

rashi.heb:
*הנני עושה.* 
ת"י הא אנא עביד גמירא ויש לפותרו ל' עישוי כמו ועסות' רשעים (מלאכי ג):
rashi.eng: *Behold, I wreak destruction.* Jonathan rendered: Behold I wreak destruction. It may also be interpreted as an expression of crushing, as in (Mal. 3:21): “And you shall crush the wicked.”

rashi.heb:
*בכל הארץ בשתם.* 
בכל מקום אשר היו שם לבשתם שם אתנם לשם ולתהלה:
rashi.eng: *throughout all the land where they suffered shame.* Every place where they were for their shame, there I will make them to be a praise and a name.

notes.170: (tn): In this line the second person pronoun is masculine plural, indicating that the exiles are addressed.
notes.172: (tn, Heb): “I will make you into a name and praise among all the peoples of the earth.” Here the word “name” carries the nuance of “good reputation.”
notes.173: (tn, Heb): “when I restore your fortunes to your eyes.” See the note on the phrase “restore them” in 2:7.
